stimulus.text:
“The great and radical vice in the construction of the existing Confederation is in the principle of LEGISLATION for STATES or GOVERNMENTS, in their CORPORATE or COLLECTIVE CAPACITIES, and as contradistinguished from the INDIVIDUALS of which they consist. . . . Except as to the rule of apportionment, the United States have an indefinite discretion to make requisitions for men and money; but they have no authority to raise either by regulations extending to the individual citizens of America. The consequence of this is, that though in theory their resolutions concerning those objects are laws, constitutionally binding on the members of the Union, yet in practice they are mere recommendations, which the States observe or disregard at their option.”
— Alexander Hamilton, Federalist No. 15, December 1, 1787

books.section: Topic 3.7 The Articles of Confederation, B. The Articles of Confederation and the Critical Period

stem: Hamilton writes that carrying out any important measure required the agreement of thirteen distinct sovereign wills. That fact best explains why

options.text: the Articles were easy to amend with the agreement of the states
options.misconception: Background: amendment needed every state, which made the Articles the hardest frame to change.

options.text: important measures often stalled, since one state's refusal could block action
the states eagerly paid their requisitions
options.misconception: Hamilton says the states observed requisitions or disregarded them at their option.

options.text: Congress could raise an army quickly
options.misconception: Background: Congress could only ask the states for troops, which is why it could not raise an army.

rationales.B: Background from the books: major decisions needed nine of thirteen states and amendments needed all thirteen, so any important measure could stall when states refused to agree.
rationales.A: Background: amendment needed all thirteen states, which made the Articles nearly impossible to change.
rationales.C: Hamilton says the states observed requisitions or disregarded them at their option.
rationales.D: Background: Congress could only request troops from the states, so it could not raise an army quickly.
rationales.general:
1. Count the wills. Background: thirteen sovereign states had to agree for an important measure to work.
2. Background: major decisions needed nine votes, and amendments needed all thirteen.
3. When any state could block action, most important measures stalled.
4. Background: the impost is the proof, since two states killed a tax the other eleven wanted.
Remember: thirteen vetoes are not a government; they are a recipe for standing still.
